grading: exactly one correct option per question; each of four choices includes specific feedback; score computed only after submission

questions.question: A feed refresh succeeds, but a known indicator is not blocked. The external resource is in hash-db mode and shows category 192. What should be checked next?

choices.text: Change the refresh interval to one minute and restart the update daemon.
choices.feedback: A shorter refresh interval does not fix a missing policy reference; first prove the feed is being used.

choices.text: Replace the publisher URL with the same feed using plain-text mode.
choices.feedback: Changing to plain-text can break a hash database feed and does not establish policy use.

choices.text: Confirm the active Web Filter profile references category 192.
choices.feedback: Correct. A fetched feed and a Web Filter profile reference are separate stages; the category must be consumed by the active profile.

choices.text: Create a firewall address object for every hostname in the feed.
choices.feedback: Manual address objects create a different control path and defeat the intended hash-feed workflow.

questions.question: Which configuration choice selects the hash database interpretation for the external resource?

choices.text: Set threat-feed-hash-mode to hash-db on the external-resource object.
choices.feedback: Correct. FortiOS exposes hash-db versus plain-text-db on the external-resource object; the publisher's feed format must match.

choices.text: Set the update method to push and leave the hash mode unchanged.
choices.feedback: Push changes delivery method, not the database interpretation used to parse the feed.

choices.text: Set the resource type to malware and reference it from IPS.
choices.feedback: Malware hash feeds are a different resource use case and do not create a Web Filter URL/SNI category.

choices.text: Set the server identity check to basic and change the category.
choices.feedback: Certificate verification and category selection do not switch the feed parser into hash-db mode.

questions.question: A HTTPS feed intermittently fails after a certificate renewal. Which evidence most directly tests server identity validation?

choices.text: Check the firewall policy hit count for the user's web session.
choices.feedback: Policy hits show traffic handling, not whether the external-resource TLS session trusts the feed server.

choices.text: Compare the URL category with the antivirus signature database version.
choices.feedback: Antivirus signatures do not validate the TLS identity of the external feed endpoint.

choices.text: Inspect the SD-WAN rule selected for the user's browser session.
choices.feedback: SD-WAN can affect the path, but it does not prove certificate trust or hostname matching.

choices.text: Review the feed certificate chain and hostname match for full identity checking.
choices.feedback: Correct. Full checking validates the certificate and verifies that the domain matches the server certificate.

questions.question: After a FortiOS 7.6.8 upgrade, administrator SSO fails with 'Single Sign-On Failed' while local login remains available. What is the safest first response?

choices.text: Rebuild all Web Filter external resources and reload hash databases.
choices.feedback: External-resource configuration is unrelated to administrator SSO and should not be changed as a first response.

choices.text: Use the documented local or RADIUS/LDAP/TACACS+ administrator path and investigate the release-specific SSO issue.
choices.feedback: Correct. Preserve administrative access through a confirmed local or remote non-SSO account, then investigate the documented 7.6.8 SSO failure.

choices.text: Disable all administrator authentication and expose HTTPS management on the WAN.
choices.feedback: Disabling authentication or exposing management increases risk and is not a controlled recovery method.

choices.text: Replace the IdP signing certificate before collecting the failed login evidence.
choices.feedback: Certificate rotation without evidence can make a release-specific regression harder to isolate.

questions.question: A factory-default FortiGate should discover FortiManager through DHCP Option 240/241, but it never contacts the manager. Which prerequisite is most important to verify?

choices.text: Confirm the model device already has a live device configuration revision.
choices.feedback: A model revision is important for installation, but it does not make DHCP options work on an interface that will not accept them.

choices.text: Confirm the selected WAN interface is DHCP-client in factory-default state.
choices.feedback: Correct. Fortinet limits this ZTP method to factory-default models whose selected WAN interface is already a DHCP client.

choices.text: Confirm the policy package uses only global address objects.
choices.feedback: Policy object scope is evaluated later; it does not control initial manager discovery.

choices.text: Confirm the FortiGate has completed a firmware upgrade before discovery.
choices.feedback: ZTP is intended to provision a new device; upgrading first is not a discovery prerequisite.

questions.question: A one-time CLI script must create interfaces on a FortiGate-VM before other templates are installed. Which mechanism fits this requirement?

choices.text: Assign a Pre-Run CLI/Jinja template to the offline model device.
choices.feedback: Correct. Pre-Run CLI/Jinja templates are model-device-only, run once against the model Device Database, and are then unassigned.

choices.text: Assign a Post-VDOM CLI template to the device group.
choices.feedback: Post-VDOM templates run after the policy package and are not the one-time model bootstrap stage.

choices.text: Run a CLI script from the live device after policy installation.
choices.feedback: A live-device script runs too late to create prerequisites needed by earlier provisioning steps.

choices.text: Attach a normal CLI template to the ADOM global layer.
choices.feedback: A normal ADOM template is not the model-only one-time pre-run mechanism.

questions.question: A model device has a policy package assigned, but the package is targeted only at a device group. What should the engineer do before the real FortiGate comes online?

choices.text: Wait for auto-link to install the group package automatically.
choices.feedback: Fortinet documents that a package targeted at a device group is not automatically installed during auto-link.

choices.text: Convert the policy package to a global database object.
choices.feedback: Global object scope does not change the documented auto-link package-install behavior.

choices.text: Disable auto-link and retrieve the real device configuration first.
choices.feedback: Retrieving a new live configuration is not possible before the device is online and is not the required step.

choices.text: Install the package explicitly before bringing the real device online.
choices.feedback: Correct. Pre-install the package to catch errors; model-device auto-link does not automatically install a group-targeted package.

questions.question: After upgrading FortiManager, an LDAPS configuration without ca-cert disappears. Which upgrade-preparation action matches the documented Community case?

choices.text: Change the LDAP port from 636 to 389 before upgrading.
choices.feedback: Changing to cleartext LDAP avoids neither the upgrade condition nor the security requirement for LDAPS.

choices.text: Disable all remote authentication servers until the upgrade finishes.
choices.feedback: Disabling authentication does not preserve the configuration and can remove administrative access paths.

choices.text: Assign a valid CA certificate that issued the LDAP server certificate before upgrading.
choices.feedback: Correct. The Community case states that LDAPS configurations without ca-cert are deleted on affected upgrades; configure the issuing CA first.

choices.text: Replace the LDAP server with a RADIUS server using the same address.
choices.feedback: Changing protocols does not preserve the LDAPS object and introduces an unrelated migration.

questions.question: A FortiAnalyzer alert is visible, but no FortiGate action runs. Which missing configuration is the most likely next checkpoint?

choices.text: Enable Archive-log indexing on the FortiAnalyzer ADOM.
choices.feedback: Archive logs are not the source used by alert handlers; indexing them does not create the FortiGate trigger.

choices.text: Create the matching alert-handler trigger on FortiGate and ensure FAZ logging is configured.
choices.feedback: Correct. FAZ sends a notification, but FortiGate requires its own matching trigger and FAZ logging configuration before the action can run.

choices.text: Change the alert handler from Basic to Correlation after it has been saved.
choices.feedback: Fortinet does not allow changing a saved handler type; recreate it only if the detection semantics are wrong.

choices.text: Move the incident to a different FortiAnalyzer ADOM.
choices.feedback: Moving ADOMs can change scope but does not create the required FortiGate automation trigger.

questions.question: A rule matches only records that have already been moved to Archive logs. Why does the alert handler not fire?

choices.text: Alert handlers generate alerts from Analytics logs, not Archive logs.
choices.feedback: Correct. The documented boundary is Analytics logs; Archive-only records do not feed the handler.

choices.text: Archive logs are evaluated only after a FortiGate automation stitch runs.
choices.feedback: Automation stitches are downstream response actions, not an Archive-log indexing mechanism.

choices.text: Correlation handlers cannot evaluate any log fields from FortiGate.
choices.feedback: Correlation handlers can evaluate sequences of rules; the issue is the log storage class.

choices.text: Notification profiles must be attached to the Archive log database.
choices.feedback: Notification profiles are separate handler objects and do not change the Analytics/Archive source boundary.

questions.question: A detection requires event A, then event B within a sequence. Which handler type is appropriate?

choices.text: A basic handler with two rules because basic rules execute in order.
choices.feedback: Basic handler rules have OR relationships; they do not encode ordered sequences.

choices.text: A notification profile with two recipients and a shared data selector.
choices.feedback: Notification profiles control delivery, not detection logic or event ordering.

choices.text: A basic handler with one OR rule and a shorter refresh interval.
choices.feedback: Changing refresh timing does not make basic rules evaluate a sequence.

choices.text: A correlation handler with sequence operators such as FOLLOWED_BY.
choices.feedback: Correct. Correlation handlers support sequence operators such as FOLLOWED_BY and NOT_FOLLOWED_BY.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the FortiAnalyzer Automation Stitch integration?

choices.text: FortiAnalyzer directly executes the FortiGate CLI script when an alert rule matches.
choices.feedback: FAZ does not directly execute arbitrary FortiGate CLI scripts; the FortiGate owns the action.

choices.text: An alert handler automatically creates every required FortiGate trigger and action.
choices.feedback: Fortinet requires the FortiGate trigger to be configured for each handler with Automation Stitch enabled.

choices.text: FortiAnalyzer notifies FortiGate, and the FortiGate's configured trigger invokes its local action.
choices.feedback: Correct. The integration is a notification bridge; the FortiGate trigger and action complete the response.

choices.text: FortiGate sends its automation action to FortiAnalyzer for execution in the ADOM.
choices.feedback: Execution direction is reversed; FortiAnalyzer generates the alert and notifies FortiGate.

questions.question: The ICL fails, but both FortiSwitch peers are still forwarding. What does split-brain detection protect against?

choices.text: It moves all traffic to the downstream switch's standalone STP root.
choices.feedback: STP root selection is not the documented MCLAG split-brain response.

choices.text: It disables LACP on both peers until the ICL is repaired.
choices.feedback: Both peers do not have to lose LACP; one is isolated to avoid dual-active forwarding.

choices.text: It makes one peer dormant while the other remains active and forwarding.
choices.feedback: Correct. Split-brain detection prevents both peers from continuing to forward independently after ICL loss.

choices.text: It converts the MCLAG into two independent access VLANs.
choices.feedback: MCLAG does not automatically redesign VLAN topology when the ICL fails.

questions.question: Both peers have split-brain priority 50. Which peer becomes dormant when the ICL-only split-brain condition is detected?

choices.text: The peer with the higher numerical MAC address becomes dormant.
choices.feedback: The documented tie-break is the lower numerical MAC, not the higher one.

choices.text: The peer with the lower numerical MAC address becomes dormant.
choices.feedback: Correct. Lower priority value wins the dormant state; equal priorities fall back to the lower numerical MAC address.

choices.text: The peer with the greater number of downstream LACP members becomes dormant.
choices.feedback: Member count is not the documented tie-break mechanism.

choices.text: The peer with the higher firmware build number becomes dormant.
choices.feedback: Firmware build number is not used as the split-brain peer selection criterion.

questions.question: A peer reboots and the other peer remains online. Which release behavior helps avoid mistaking this for an ICL-only split-brain event?

choices.text: FortiSwitchOS 7.4.1 distinguishes a peer down/restart from an ICL down event.
choices.feedback: Correct. Starting in 7.4.1, FortiSwitchOS distinguishes peer down/restart from ICL down, with a dual-homed FortiSwitch requirement.

choices.text: FortiSwitchOS 6.2.2 disables MCLAG whenever any peer reboots.
choices.feedback: 6.2.2 added CLI split-brain detection; it does not disable MCLAG on every reboot.

choices.text: FortiSwitchOS 7.6.2 forces every third-party switch to become the active peer.
choices.feedback: Third-party topology support does not transfer active-peer control to the third-party switch.

choices.text: FortiSwitchOS 8.0.0 removes the ICL and relies on STP convergence.
choices.feedback: The ICL remains a core MCLAG component in the documented topology.

questions.question: A FortiSwitchOS 7.6.2 design dual-homes to third-party switches. Which caveat matters for split-brain design?

choices.text: Split-brain detection is unavailable whenever any third-party switch is present.
choices.feedback: Fortinet documents third-party dual-homed support in specified topologies; it does not remove all split-brain detection.

choices.text: The ICL must be converted to an untagged access port.
choices.feedback: ICL configuration remains an LACP trunk, not a generic access port.

choices.text: The downstream third-party switch chooses the dormant FortiSwitch by STP priority.
choices.feedback: Peer selection remains a FortiSwitch function; STP priority on the third-party switch is not the documented tie-break.

choices.text: The split-brain priority command is not supported in the documented third-party topology.
choices.feedback: Correct. Fortinet notes that mclag-split-brain-priority is not supported when third-party switches are present.

questions.question: An external portal accepts the user's credentials but FortiGate never completes the pending login. Which field must the portal preserve from the original redirect?

choices.text: The magic value associated with the pending captive-portal session.
choices.feedback: Correct. The external portal must return the original magic value with the username and password to /fgtauth.

choices.text: The AP radio's BSSID and channel assignment.
choices.feedback: BSSID and channel are radio association data, not the captive-portal transaction token.

choices.text: The DHCP server identifier from the client's lease.
choices.feedback: DHCP server identity does not bind the browser's return to the pending authentication session.

choices.text: The FortiAP serial number used during CAPWAP discovery.
choices.feedback: AP serial number is unrelated to the documented /fgtauth POST fields.

questions.question: A client associates and authenticates successfully but cannot reach the Internet. Which next check best separates identity success from authorization?

choices.text: Rebuild the FortiAP radio profile and change the channel width.
choices.feedback: Radio settings do not explain a successful authentication followed by denied routed traffic.

choices.text: Disable WPA3 and force every client to use an open SSID.
choices.feedback: Removing wireless encryption is unsafe and does not correct group or policy authorization.

choices.text: Verify the selected user group and the post-authentication firewall policy.
choices.feedback: Correct. Portal success must be followed by a permitted group and matching firewall policy/NAT path.

choices.text: Reset the AP to factory defaults and repeat CAPWAP discovery.
choices.feedback: Factory reset is disproportionate when association and portal authentication already work.

questions.question: Which setting protects credentials returned from an external captive portal to FortiGate?

choices.text: Enable client isolation on the SSID and leave the portal HTTP endpoint unchanged.
choices.feedback: Client isolation does not encrypt the browser's credential POST to FortiGate.

choices.text: Enable auth-secure-http under config user setting.
choices.feedback: Correct. Fortinet documents auth-secure-http enable to secure the credential submission.

choices.text: Set the SSID traffic mode to bridge and disable the portal redirect.
choices.feedback: Disabling the portal removes the authentication flow rather than protecting it.

choices.text: Use the portal's original HTTP URL as the external-web field.
choices.feedback: The external-web field is the host name, and the credential return should use HTTPS.

questions.question: A FortiAP 231K repeatedly restarts cwWtpd/lldpd and CAPWAP fails. What does the restart log prove?

choices.text: It proves the portal's user-group mapping is invalid.
choices.feedback: Portal group mapping is downstream of AP control-plane stability and is not shown by daemon restart logs.

choices.text: It proves the RADIUS server rejected the client password.
choices.feedback: RADIUS rejection would require authentication evidence, not only daemon restart messages.

choices.text: It proves the external portal lost its magic value.
choices.feedback: Magic values exist in captive-portal transactions and do not explain AP daemon restarts.

choices.text: It proves the daemons restarted, but not the underlying cause.
choices.feedback: Correct. The Community thread explicitly notes that restart messages alone do not identify the cause; firmware/build and certificate compatibility need checking.

questions.question: FortiGate logs show the Quarantine via FortiNAC stitch fired, but the endpoint still reaches production. What is the most likely missing dependency?

choices.text: The FortiGate needs a new SD-WAN health-check target.
choices.feedback: SD-WAN health checks do not enforce a NAC-disabled MAC state.

choices.text: The FortiNAC connector must be moved to an Archive ADOM.
choices.feedback: ADOM placement is unrelated to the FortiNAC access-layer isolation behavior.

choices.text: The FortiNAC disabled-host isolation and access-edge Dead End VLAN are not configured.
choices.feedback: Correct. FortiNAC can disable the MAC, but the AP/Switch or FortiGate access edge must enforce the disabled-host state.

choices.text: The endpoint must receive a new DHCP lease from FortiGate.
choices.feedback: A DHCP lease change does not create the required quarantine VLAN or port enforcement.

questions.question: A webhook triggers quarantine for the wrong endpoint. Which part of the request should be validated first?

choices.text: The source IP, MAC address and FortiClient UID in the webhook payload.
choices.feedback: Correct. The webhook payload identifies the endpoint; an incorrect MAC can quarantine the wrong host.

choices.text: The FortiGate's Web Filter category and external-resource refresh timer.
choices.feedback: Web Filter objects do not identify the endpoint for the FortiNAC quarantine action.

choices.text: The FortiSwitch MCLAG split-brain priority and ICL LACP state.
choices.feedback: MCLAG health is an access-layer availability concern, not the webhook identity payload.

choices.text: The FortiAnalyzer notification profile and Archive log retention.
choices.feedback: FAZ alert delivery and Archive retention do not validate the MAC supplied to the action.

questions.question: Which observation proves FortiNAC actually changed the endpoint state rather than only receiving the FortiGate trigger?

choices.text: The FortiGate system event says the automation stitch was triggered.
choices.feedback: The FortiGate event proves the trigger ran, not that the NAC host record changed.

choices.text: The FortiNAC Host View shows the host quarantined and its MAC disabled.
choices.feedback: Correct. Host View confirms the endpoint is quarantined and the MAC is disabled.

choices.text: The webhook client received an HTTP response from FortiGate.
choices.feedback: A webhook response proves request handling, not the downstream NAC state change.

choices.text: The FortiGate automation page shows a nonzero last-triggered timestamp.
choices.feedback: A last-triggered time proves activation, not access-layer enforcement.

questions.question: A FortiNAC domain join reports WBC_ERR_WINBIND_NOT_AVAILABLE and cannot obtain domain details. Which dependency should be tested before changing user credentials?

choices.text: The MCLAG ICL LACP state between access switches.
choices.feedback: MCLAG affects switching availability but does not resolve a Winbind domain lookup error.

choices.text: The FortiAnalyzer Analytics log retention setting.
choices.feedback: Analytics retention is unrelated to the FortiNAC domain-join dependency.

choices.text: The FortiGate external-resource category assignment.
choices.feedback: External-resource categories are unrelated to Winbind or AD discovery.

choices.text: DNS resolution of the Active Directory domain controller and domain.
choices.feedback: Correct. The Community case identifies DNS resolution as a cause of Winbind being unable to locate the domain controller.

questions.question: A FortiNAC-F SAML user is sent back to the portal start page. The ACS POST receives a generic 302 to the portal FQDN; FortiAuthenticator logs IdP success, but FortiNAC-F has no SAMLUtils lines, no SSO user and no CoA. Which mismatch is most likely?

choices.text: The FortiNAC-F host record has the wrong MAC address.
choices.feedback: MAC identity matters for registration enforcement, but it does not explain why the ACS POST is redirected before SAML processing.

choices.text: The SP URL and captive-portal FQDN are different.
choices.feedback: Correct. The ACS URL is built from the SP URL; if it differs from the portal FQDN, FortiNAC-F can return a generic portal redirect without processing the assertion.

choices.text: The IdP signing certificate has expired.
choices.feedback: The IdP has returned a successful response; the missing SAMLUtils processing lines point to the ACS hostname path, not a signature rejection.

choices.text: The FortiSwitch ICL is down and one peer is dormant.
choices.feedback: An MCLAG failure can affect access, but it does not explain a generic HTTP redirect at the SAML ACS endpoint.

questions.question: SAML signature validation succeeds, but the user lands in the wrong FortiNAC access group. What should be inspected?

choices.text: The FortiGate interface's outgoing bandwidth limit.
choices.feedback: Bandwidth limits affect egress shaping, not SAML group selection.

choices.text: The RADIUS shared secret on every switch in the fabric.
choices.feedback: RADIUS secrets can affect later CoA/authentication, but not the validated SAML claim mapping itself.

choices.text: The SAML assertion attribute names/values and FortiNAC custom group mapping.
choices.feedback: Correct. FortiNAC assigns groups and access policies from SAML attribute values; verify the claim and mapping.

choices.text: The FortiNAC server's external DNS forwarder cache only.
choices.feedback: DNS may affect portal reachability, but it does not explain a valid assertion mapped to the wrong group.

questions.question: The ACS receives a SAML response but signature verification fails after an IdP certificate rollover. What is the best corrective path?

choices.text: Import the correct IdP signing certificate and trust chain, then validate the connector metadata.
choices.feedback: Correct. The SP must trust the signing certificate used by the IdP and validate the expected metadata.

choices.text: Change the captive portal to open authentication and bypass SAML.
choices.feedback: Open authentication bypasses the identity requirement and is not a secure certificate repair.

choices.text: Disable CoA so the browser can complete the IdP login.
choices.feedback: CoA is a later network-enforcement step; it does not repair a failed SAML signature.

choices.text: Replace the FortiNAC-F user group with a local MAC group.
choices.feedback: MAC groups are not a replacement for the IdP user attribute mapping.

questions.question: A primary-node SAML test succeeds. What additional test is required before declaring the integration production-ready?

choices.text: Test only a second browser on the same primary node.
choices.feedback: A second browser does not test the HA control-plane transition.

choices.text: Verify the FortiGate Web Filter profile contains the SAML group name.
choices.feedback: Web Filter profiles do not prove the FortiNAC-F SAML flow works after failover.

choices.text: Disable the secondary node's captive portal service.
choices.feedback: Disabling the secondary removes the failover path rather than validating it.

choices.text: Repeat the login and registration flow after HA failover on the active secondary.
choices.feedback: Correct. The Community case explicitly recommends repeating the SAML/registration evidence after failover.

questions.question: A Remote LDAP group has Include for FSSO enabled, but the option was unavailable for another group. Which retrieval mode is required?

choices.text: Specify an LDAP filter with dynamic group membership.
choices.feedback: The new Include for FSSO option is documented for imported remote LDAP users, not the LDAP-filter retrieval mode.

choices.text: Set the group type to Remote RADIUS and import the users.
choices.feedback: Remote RADIUS groups are a different identity source and do not satisfy the LDAP prerequisite.

choices.text: Set User retrieval to a list of imported remote LDAP users.
choices.feedback: Correct. The option is available only when User retrieval is set to a list of imported remote LDAP users.

choices.text: Create a local MAC group and add the LDAP users manually.
choices.feedback: Manual MAC groups do not expose remote LDAP group membership to FSSO.

questions.question: A group is flagged Include for FSSO, but it never appears in the FortiGate filter picker. Which second setting must be checked?

choices.text: Include locally-defined remote LDAP groups under FSSO User Group Membership.
choices.feedback: Correct. FortiAuthenticator requires both per-group inclusion and the global FSSO group-membership inclusion setting.

choices.text: Enable FortiToken push without an Access-Challenge in the RADIUS policy.
choices.feedback: FortiToken push is a separate RADIUS authentication behavior and does not publish LDAP groups to FSSO.

choices.text: Change the remote LDAP server from LDAPS to plain LDAP.
choices.feedback: Changing transport security is not required to expose a correctly imported LDAP group.

choices.text: Enable FortiGate SSL deep inspection for the LDAP server.
choices.feedback: SSL deep inspection is unrelated to FAC's local FSSO group inclusion setting.

questions.question: A user can authenticate successfully against LDAP, but a FortiGate policy using an FSSO group does not match. What does the successful LDAP bind fail to prove?

choices.text: It proves the FortiGate has learned a current logon session and group.
choices.feedback: LDAP authentication does not itself prove FSSO session or group projection.

choices.text: It proves only that LDAP authentication worked, not that group projection and FSSO session learning succeeded.
choices.feedback: Correct. Authentication, imported group membership, FSSO filter publication and session learning are separate stages.

choices.text: It proves the firewall policy has the correct source interface and service.
choices.feedback: Policy interface and service matching are independent from the LDAP bind.

choices.text: It proves the imported LDAP user list is synchronized and current.
choices.feedback: A successful bind does not prove the imported list or group sync is current.

questions.question: A FortiClient IKEv2 EAP-TTLS login reports EAPPasswordError, while LDAP, FortiToken and the RADIUS policy are already working. Which diagnostic boundary is most relevant?

choices.text: Treat the error as proof that the remote LDAP password is wrong.
choices.feedback: The Community case says LDAP was already working; the generic client error does not prove a bad password.

choices.text: Change the FSSO Remote LDAP Group filter to a local user group.
choices.feedback: FSSO group filters do not control the EAP-TTLS/OTP challenge exchange.

choices.text: Disable certificate validation on every remote authentication server.
choices.feedback: Disabling trust validation is unsafe and not supported by the reported symptom.

choices.text: Inspect RADIUS challenge and OTP-concatenation behavior separately from LDAP password validation.
choices.feedback: Correct. The discussion identifies OTP concatenation/challenge behavior as a separate RADIUS/EAP path.

questions.question: A root FortiPAM and two gateways form a chain to an isolated SSH target. Which gateway needs direct network access to that target?

choices.text: The root FortiPAM must reach every target and every intermediate gateway.
choices.feedback: The root needs the reverse control-plane connection, not direct access to every private target.

choices.text: Only the terminal gateway in the chain needs direct target connectivity.
choices.feedback: Correct. Fortinet explicitly states only the terminal gateway requires direct network connectivity to the target.

choices.text: Every gateway in the chain must have a route to every protected target.
choices.feedback: Intermediate gateways forward the chain; they do not all need target routes.

choices.text: The service gateway nearest the root must reach the target directly.
choices.feedback: The first gateway is not necessarily the terminal gateway; target reachability belongs at the last hop.

questions.question: A downstream gateway establishes TLS to the root, but it is not dynamically discovered. Which pair of settings is most directly relevant?

choices.text: Correct Root FortiPAM serial and an allowlisted certificate Common Name.
choices.feedback: Correct. The root serial identifies the central FortiPAM, while the gateway ID whitelist checks the downstream certificate CN.

choices.text: Matching SSH port and target username on every secret.
choices.feedback: Target service credentials do not establish the reverse gateway's identity or root association.

choices.text: Matching RDP NLA realm and a shared secret password.
choices.feedback: RDP realm and secret passwords are not part of the reverse-service mTLS discovery check.

choices.text: Matching gateway interface MTU and target DNS suffix.
choices.feedback: MTU and DNS can affect reachability, but they do not satisfy root serial or CN allowlisting.

questions.question: Which default transport configuration is documented for the FortiPAM Reverse Service?

choices.text: TCP 443 with TLS 1.1 and a server-only certificate.
choices.feedback: Port 443 is used in some data-plane examples, not the default reverse control-plane listener.

choices.text: UDP 8443 with TLS 1.2 and a shared gateway password.
choices.feedback: Reverse Service uses a TCP listening port and certificate-based mTLS, not UDP/password-only authentication.

choices.text: TCP 8443 with TLS 1.3 as the default maximum and client CA validation.
choices.feedback: Correct. The documented default is port 8443, TLS 1.3 maximum, server certificate and client CA.

choices.text: TCP 22 with SSH host keys and a gateway API token.
choices.feedback: SSH is a target protocol and not the reverse-service mTLS transport.

questions.question: The dynamic gateway chain is visible at the root, but launching a target fails. Which next check is most precise?

choices.text: Rebuild the root gateway certificate before checking any network path.
choices.feedback: A discovered chain indicates the mTLS registration succeeded; replacing certificates first may destroy working trust.

choices.text: Change the root FortiPAM serial number to the terminal gateway serial.
choices.feedback: The root serial identifies the central FortiPAM and should not be replaced by the terminal gateway serial.

choices.text: Remove the Gateway ID Whitelist to permit all downstream certificates.
choices.feedback: Removing the allowlist weakens trust and does not solve a target data-path failure.

choices.text: Verify the terminal gateway's route, DNS, firewall and target service reachability.
choices.feedback: Correct. Once discovery succeeds, the terminal gateway's direct target path is the next independent boundary.

questions.question: An incident exists, but no Automation Policy sends an email. Which first check most directly tests whether the policy should match?

choices.text: Compare incident rule, severity, timestamp and affected item with the policy gates.
choices.feedback: Correct. Rule, severity, time range and affected item are the core match gates before the action is evaluated.

choices.text: Increase the ClickHouse warm-storage allocation and restart the collector.
choices.feedback: Storage capacity may affect event retention, but it does not correct a policy that does not match.

choices.text: Change the incident from Analytics to Archive log storage.
choices.feedback: FortiSIEM Automation Policies route incidents; Archive storage is not the relevant match control.

choices.text: Create a second incident with the same source IP and event name.
choices.feedback: Duplicate incidents can add noise and do not prove the existing policy's scope.

questions.question: A policy applies to a device group except one excluded device group. Where is the exclusion represented?

choices.text: In the event handler's correlation sequence.
choices.feedback: Correlation sequences create incidents; they do not hold the Automation Policy's explicit exclusion list.

choices.text: In the action's SMTP recipient list.
choices.feedback: Recipients affect who receives an email, not which device incidents match the policy.

choices.text: In the FortiSIEM global device discovery schedule.
choices.feedback: Discovery schedules do not define the policy's affected-item scope.

choices.text: In the Affected Items NOT Selections column.
choices.feedback: Correct. The documented policy editor lets selected groups be moved to the NOT Selections column.

questions.question: A policy matches and should create a case, but the case action is unavailable. Which prerequisite pair should be checked?

choices.text: A FortiGate REST API admin and a FortiAnalyzer ADOM.
choices.feedback: Those objects are used by other products and do not enable FortiSIEM case creation.

choices.text: A FortiSIEM Analysts group and a Case Management Policy.
choices.feedback: Correct. FortiSIEM requires an Analysts group and a Case Management Policy; the action is not available at Org level.

choices.text: A FortiSASE API connector and a FortiGuard DLP pattern.
choices.feedback: CASB objects are unrelated to FortiSIEM incident case management.

choices.text: A FortiNAC security fabric connector and a Dead End VLAN.
choices.feedback: NAC quarantine prerequisites do not affect FortiSIEM case actions.

questions.question: An incident is created and quickly auto-cleared. The policy is configured not to notify on automatically cleared incidents. What should happen?

choices.text: The policy should send an email twice to preserve the incident history.
choices.feedback: The policy exception is not a duplicate-email mechanism.

choices.text: The incident should be deleted before the analytics rule runs.
choices.feedback: Auto-clearing occurs after detection; deleting the incident is not the documented exception behavior.

choices.text: The policy should create a case but suppress only the webhook action.
choices.feedback: The exception applies to the policy's notification trigger, not only one action type.

choices.text: The exception should suppress the notification/action for that cleared incident.
choices.feedback: Correct. FortiSIEM documents an exception to not notify when an incident is cleared automatically.

questions.question: A file is uploaded directly to a SaaS tenant and later flagged by API-based CASB DLP. Which statement best describes the inspection plane?

choices.text: The DLP engine must have been inline on every packet before the upload completed.
choices.feedback: That describes inline inspection, not the API-based CASB data plane.

choices.text: API-based CASB queries onboarded SaaS accounts through provider APIs and evaluates file/activity data.
choices.feedback: Correct. The API connector supplies visibility into onboarded SaaS files and activity without requiring all packets to traverse SIA.

choices.text: The alert proves the file was blocked before it reached the cloud application.
choices.feedback: An API-based alert does not by itself prove pre-upload inline blocking.

choices.text: The SaaS tenant is inspected only when a user connects through an IPsec tunnel.
choices.feedback: An IPsec tunnel is not the prerequisite for the SaaS provider API integration.

questions.question: A custom pattern misses large compressed documents even though the regex is correct. Which settings are most likely to explain the gap?

choices.text: The SIA tunnel port and the endpoint posture tag.
choices.feedback: SIA transport and posture tags do not define the API CASB pattern's file-size boundary.

choices.text: The SD-WAN member priority and the branch underlay bandwidth.
choices.feedback: SD-WAN steering is unrelated to the CASB file scanning limits.

choices.text: The FortiGuard pattern category and the web-filter cache.
choices.feedback: FortiGuard pattern categories do not override the custom pattern's configured size limits.

choices.text: The custom pattern's compressed and uncompressed file-size limits.
choices.feedback: Correct. The custom pattern exposes separate maximum compressed and uncompressed file sizes.

questions.question: A custom regex exists, but no DLP alert appears for a supported SaaS file. Which policy object binds the pattern to app activity?

choices.text: The Data Policy that selects the cloud application, file types and file activities.
choices.feedback: Correct. Data policies bind patterns to cloud applications, file types, access permissions and activity triggers.

choices.text: The SIA tunnel profile that chooses the user's closest point of presence.
choices.feedback: SIA steering selects a traffic path and does not bind API DLP patterns.

choices.text: The endpoint posture tag group that matches device compliance.
choices.feedback: Posture tags affect access control and are not the API CASB DLP data policy.

choices.text: The private-access application definition that maps an internal FQDN.
choices.feedback: Private-access application definitions describe private resources, not SaaS file DLP.

questions.question: The API connector reports healthy, but a file is never scanned. What is the most useful next investigation?

choices.text: Increase the branch IPsec MTU and change the default route.
choices.feedback: Branch MTU is not the primary dependency for a SaaS API file scan.

choices.text: Disable all FortiGuard patterns and rely only on inline IPS.
choices.feedback: Inline IPS is a different inspection plane and does not replace API-based CASB data policies.

choices.text: Check account onboarding, API permissions, file-size boundary and data-policy activity scope.
choices.feedback: Correct. Connector health alone does not prove account enumeration, file eligibility or policy activity matching.

choices.text: Rebuild the user's FortiClient endpoint certificate.
choices.feedback: Endpoint certificates do not normally determine the SaaS tenant API connector's file scope.

questions.question: A session uses the expected WAN member but bulk traffic still starves voice traffic during congestion. Which layer should be examined next?

choices.text: The firewall shaping policy, shaper priority and advanced shaping profile.
choices.feedback: Correct. Member selection succeeded; QoS classification and egress scheduling are the next independent layer.

choices.text: The SD-WAN health-check target name and probe interval only.
choices.feedback: Health checks influence member eligibility, not the shaper's priority or bandwidth guarantee.

choices.text: The IPsec phase-1 peer ID and remote gateway certificate.
choices.feedback: VPN authentication is unrelated if the session already uses the expected member.

choices.text: The routing protocol's router ID and route-reflector cluster ID.
choices.feedback: Routing identifiers do not determine the configured traffic shaper priority.

questions.question: An advanced shaping profile allocates percentages to traffic groups. Which configured value determines each group's effective speed limit?

choices.text: The FortiGate's total system memory and NP session count.
choices.feedback: Memory and NP capacity do not set the interface bandwidth base for a shaping profile.

choices.text: The remote site's BGP local preference and AS path length.
choices.feedback: BGP path attributes may influence routing but do not define the shaping percentage base.

choices.text: The outgoing bandwidth limit configured on the egress interface.
choices.feedback: Correct. Fortinet states each group is shaped to its assigned speed based on the interface's outgoing bandwidth limit.

choices.text: The SD-WAN SLA latency threshold and packet-loss threshold.
choices.feedback: SLA thresholds influence path eligibility/steering, not the profile's configured bandwidth base.

questions.question: Why may a high-priority HTTP/HTTPS flow and a low-priority FTP flow show similar throughput in an idle lab?

choices.text: The SD-WAN rule automatically removes the shaping policy when no traffic exists.
choices.feedback: The shaping policy is not automatically removed when the interface is idle.

choices.text: The low-priority shaper always receives a higher guarantee than high-priority traffic.
choices.feedback: Low priority does not imply a higher guarantee than high priority.

choices.text: The interface ignores traffic shaping until an SLA probe fails.
choices.feedback: SLA probe failure is not a prerequisite for traffic shaping.

choices.text: Priority differences are most observable when competing traffic creates congestion.
choices.feedback: Correct. Priority determines relative scheduling under contention; an idle link may not expose the difference.

questions.question: An SLA probe enters an IPsec tunnel and debug flow reports reverse path check fail, drop. What should be checked before tuning QoS?

choices.text: The traffic shaping profile's low-priority group percentage.
choices.feedback: Shaping cannot repair a probe discarded by reverse-path validation before egress scheduling.

choices.text: The route back to the probe source and the interface on which the packet arrived.
choices.feedback: Correct. The Community case traced the drop to a return route pointing through the default WAN rather than the incoming tunnel.

choices.text: The FortiAnalyzer alert handler's Automation Stitch flag.
choices.feedback: FAZ alert handling is unrelated to the FortiGate packet's reverse-path decision.

choices.text: The FortiPAM gateway certificate Common Name.
choices.feedback: Gateway certificate identity is unrelated to the IPsec probe's RPF check.

questions.question: A FortiManager 7.6.8 install preview includes udp-not-quic allow, but the target FortiGate rejects the command or verification cannot read it. What is the best next action?

choices.text: Apply the same CLI workaround globally to every device in the ADOM.
choices.feedback: A global workaround can damage models that support the attribute and exceeds the evidence from the case.

choices.text: Assume the failure is only caused by 2 GB RAM and replace the appliance.
choices.feedback: The Community thread includes reports beyond 2 GB models, so memory alone is not a reliable diagnosis.

choices.text: Compare the exact model/firmware capability and scope any workaround to the affected device.
choices.feedback: Correct. The thread shows model/firmware capability and verification boundaries; keep any workaround device-scoped.

choices.text: Disable verification for the entire policy package and retry the install.
choices.feedback: Disabling verification hides a mismatch instead of resolving whether the target supports the setting.

questions.question: After aligning the SP URL and portal FQDN, the ACS POST returns 302 without a generic redirect body. FortiNAC-F logs Signature verified, SAML Authentication status true and Registration complete; the controller records CoA SUCCESS. What does this evidence establish?

choices.text: The SAML assertion was processed and the host-registration/CoA path completed.
choices.feedback: Correct. The SAMLUtils success, registration completion and CoA success show the authentication-to-enforcement transaction progressed; confirm the host is in the production VLAN and repeat after HA failover.

choices.text: The IdP failed to return an assertion, so the browser must retry.
choices.feedback: The ACS POST and signature-validation messages prove a SAML response was received and processed.

choices.text: The RADIUS server rejected the user before group assignment.
choices.feedback: A controller CoA with SUCCESS contradicts a RADIUS rejection as the primary result in this evidence set.

choices.text: The host is still Rogue because a 302 always indicates a portal failure.
choices.feedback: A 302 can be the expected response after ACS processing; inspect the body and SAMLUtils logs rather than treating every redirect as failure.
